newsitem.title: UK: CJD epidemic could reach thousands, experts warn.
newsitem.headline: CJD epidemic could reach thousands, experts warn.

text.p: The medical time bomb planted by mad cow disease may kill tens of thousands of people -- or perhaps fewer than a hundred -- British epidemiologists said on Wednesday.

It will be years before anyone knows for sure, according to the expert study of how factors still unknown will determine the size of the human epidemic resulting from the infection of British cattle herds.
The best to hope for, they said, would be a total of no more than 75 victims. The worst might be as many as 80,000.
Twelve people have so far died from a slowly incubated brain wasting disease believed to result from eating infected beef. Three more cases have been diagnosed, one of them in France.

The cattle disease is officially called Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy or BSE. Human victims suffer a new form identified last March of an older but very rare brain illness, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease or CJD.

New infections are assumed to have been stopped by tighter controls on animal feeds and slaughter house methods. But unknown numbers of people are carrying the infection and doomed to develop the disease.

Researchers at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and at the National CJD Surveillance Unit in Edinburgh, who developed the new epidemiological model, say anyone who makes firm predictions is jumping the gun.
One thing is sure. "There are going to be more cases, whatever the cause," Peter Smith of the London school told a news conference.
"We cannot yet rule out a large epidemic," said Simon Cousens of the school, who also worked on the study.
Hundreds of thousands of British cattle had BSE at the height of the epidemic, which started in 1986. Small outbreaks took place in a few other countries.

"The order requiring the destruction of cattle clinically suspected of having BSE was not introduced until August 1988 and, until then, clinically affected animals may themselves have entered the human food chain," Cousens's group wrote in a commentary in the science journal Nature.
They set out to see how many more cases there might be.

But they do not have most of the basic information that epidemiologists need. They do not know how many infected cattle were eaten, how infectious the beef might be, or whether some people are more susceptible than others.

"What we actually know at the moment is that 13 cases developed between 1994 and 1995," Cousens said. "At least 200 people need to have been infected with the agent to produce those 13 cases in 1994 and 1995."
Using a technique known as back-calculation, they set up several scenarios.
If the incubation period for the new form of CJD averages 10 years, there could be anywhere between 75 and 213 cases, they said.
But if the disease takes longer to develop -- say 25 years -- the epidemic could be just starting and will surge to tens of thousands of cases.
Much also depended, they said, on how many farmers lied about or failed to notice BSE-infected cattle -- and when.

"If under-reporting of BSE cases was common at the start of the epidemic and then declined, then we would be further into any BSE-related CJD epidemic than if under-reporting remained constant," they wrote.
